awd_titl_txt: Computational Characterization of Inter- and Intramolecular Non-Covalent Interactions
awd_abstract_narration:
With the support of the Chemical Structure, Dynamics, and Mechanisms-A (CSDM-A) Program in the Division of Chemistry, the research group of Professor Greg Tschumper at the University of Mississippi will carry out a computational chemistry study of subtle attractive interactions between molecules, specifically of non-covalent or non-bonding interactions. Although non-covalent interactions are generally much weaker, their collective contributions are central to a host of chemical processes in physics, chemistry and biology, from the structure of DNA to aerosols in the atmosphere and natural gas clathrate hydrates on the ocean floor.  The team will use computational chemistry methods based on quantum mechanics (QM) to study both fundamental aspects of non-covalent interactions as well as practical applications for organic semiconducting devices. More broadly, the potential impact of this work includes accelerating the development of novel materials for flexible electronics, clean energy technologies, water purification, water harvesting and more. This research will contribute to the education and training of science students from underrepresented groups at the graduate and undergraduate levels, and will provide research experiences for community college students through a collaboration with Dr. Jeremy Carr of Central Alabama Community College (CACC).

This research project in the Tschumper group will examine the use of halogen, chalcogen and pnictogen bonding to produce unique morphologies in nanoscale molecular assemblies for organic semiconducting devices as well as how these non-covalent interactions alter the opto-electronic properties of the components. This research team will also employ high-accuracy QM techniques to probe fundamental aspects of hydrogen bonding in clusters of water and small prototypes that provide important test systems for theoretically and experimentally studying cooperative effects associated with these non-covalent interactions. Emphasis is placed on the evaluation of spectroscopic signatures of these interactions to facilitate direct comparison to experimental measurements, and the ongoing development of the N-body:Many-body integrated QM:QM method facilitates the application of these demanding high-accuracy procedures to larger clusters with modest computational resources.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This research project, initiated at the University of Mississippi under NSF award CHE-2154403 and continued at Missouri University of Science and Technology under NSF award CHE-2452726, used advanced computational chemistry methods to investigate noncovalent interactions—the relatively weak forces that influence how molecules interact with one another. Although individually much weaker than conventional chemical bonds, these interactions are essential to understanding the structures and properties of water, biological molecules, and advanced materials. The project focused on understanding these interactions at the molecular level, developing reliable computational approaches to study them, and providing theoretical predictions to help interpret experimental measurements.

Intellectual Merit

One of the principal scientific outcomes was a better understanding of hydrogen bonding and proton transfer in small molecular clusters. Using highly accurate quantum mechanical calculations, the research team characterized the energy barriers associated with the simultaneous transfer of multiple protons around cyclic arrangements of water, hydrogen fluoride, and hydrogen chloride molecules. The results demonstrated that combining different molecular components can significantly lower these barriers compared with clusters composed of identical molecules. These findings provide new insights into the factors controlling proton movement through hydrogen-bonded networks.

The project also advanced our understanding of how water interacts with negatively charged ions. Systematic studies revealed how the size and charge of an ion influence the arrangements and binding energies of surrounding water molecules. These investigations demonstrated that hydrogen bonds between water molecules play an important role even in very small hydration networks. Related research provided the first molecular-level characterization of how water interacts with the recently discovered chloronitramide anion, a disinfection byproduct potentially present in drinking water.

Another important outcome was the characterization of competition between different types of noncovalent interactions, particularly hydrogen bonding and halogen bonding. The researchers identified molecular systems in which these interactions are energetically competitive, providing predictions that can guide experimental investigations. Collaborative studies also examined hydrogen bonding in hydrogen sulfide, combining theoretical calculations with experimental spectroscopy to reveal similarities and differences relative to water.

The project contributed to improvements in computational methods for investigating molecular clusters. The researchers developed and applied approaches that make highly accurate quantum mechanical calculations feasible for larger molecular systems. Benchmark studies provided reliable reference data for evaluating less computationally demanding methods. Additional research demonstrated that attaching argon atoms to water clusters, an experimental technique used to facilitate spectroscopic measurements, can influence the relative stability of different molecular arrangements and potentially affect experimental observations.

Broader Impacts

The knowledge generated by this project has applications beyond fundamental chemistry. Improved descriptions of hydrogen bonding and molecular interactions contribute to the development of more accurate computational models for aqueous chemistry, molecular recognition, and materials science. Collaborative investigations of organic dyes also provided insights into the electronic properties of molecules that absorb and emit near-infrared light, with potential applications in optoelectronic materials.

The project provided research and professional development opportunities for graduate students, undergraduate students, postdoctoral researchers, and educators. Research associated with the award contributed to multiple doctoral dissertations, peer-reviewed scientific publications, and presentations at national and international scientific conferences.

An important educational component involved collaborations with a community college instructor and a high school teacher. These partnerships provided opportunities for educators and community college students to participate in computational chemistry research, including work that resulted in peer-reviewed publications with community college student co-authors. Undergraduate students from institutions with limited research opportunities also participated in summer research programs, gaining experience with advanced computational tools and scientific research.

Overall, the project advanced fundamental understanding of molecular interactions, established reliable computational benchmarks for future investigations, strengthened connections between theoretical chemistry and experimental measurements, and provided valuable research experiences for students and educators.
